# The Inevitability of Privacy in CLOBs


### A logical approach to Private Orders


[Annanay Kapila](https://substack.com/@annanaykapila)


Nov 26, 2026


In


[the previous article](https://research.qfex.com/p/the-cost-of-showing-your-hand) , we discussed the downsides of broadcasting the ‘kitchen sink’ to every market participant.


In this article, we discuss the various shades of privacy available in both TradFi and crypto, and why we believe this will be the key to bootstrapping liquidity.


## The Tradeoffs Behind a Single Order


Say Alice wants to buy 100,000 shares at $100. She is worried about exposing this information to the market, so she displays 1,000 and keeps 99,000 in reserve.


Alice’s reserve is useful liquidity: somebody can trade with it. But the visible portion does more. It advertises a price, lets other traders assess the market and gives sellers a reason to send orders there. In short, it aids price discovery.


The exchange benefits from that advertisement. A book with competitive prices and substantial visible size is easier to attract business to than a book whose liquidity must be discovered by trying to trade. So an exchange may give displayed interest benefits that it withholds from concealed interest.


On most price-time priority books, refreshed display quantity moves to the back of the queue at its price. Rules differ across venues and matching algorithms, but this particular rule makes the cost of concealment clear. Crypto exchanges have another lever: they can make icebergs pay higher fees.


Alice can display more and secure priority for more quantity, or she can hide more and accept that other orders will move ahead when she replenishes. Neither choice is free.


## A Digression: Iceberg Orders and Fast Private Fills


A trader getting filled in the CME is told about their trade privately before the information is disseminated to the market. The relative speedup is proportional to the trader’s queue position; orders first in the queue get wind of a new trade before anyone else, but traders at the back of the queue get to know ‘more’ - namely that the entire level has been wiped.


For a long time, you could get the best of both worlds with iceberg orders on CME: be told first, and be told whether the whole level was wiped or not.


[See Stefan Schlamp’s post for how.](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/stefanschlamp_cme-lowlatency-hft-share-7029899919201030144-h9Sr/)


## QFEX Private Orders: Removing the Tip


An iceberg still publishes a clue: a bid that repeatedly replenishes tells observers that the apparent small buyer has more appetite behind it.


The logical next step is to remove the visible tip entirely. Many US venues operate this type of ‘dark liquidity’ as a separate liquidity pool, but at QFEX, we would rather not fragment liquidity, so we have implemented them as Private Orders in a unified CLOB.


Suppose the best displayed offer is $100.10, but another trader would sell at $100.05 if they could keep that willingness private. An exchange that insists on displaying every order may never receive the better offer.


QFEX’s private-order design lets that seller participate. Displayed and private orders share a matching engine, and ordinary taking orders can execute against both. The public book continues to show displayed liquidity; the engine can also find liquidity that has not advertised itself.


This is an obvious lift from traditional market structure. Non-displayed orders already let traders offer liquidity without publishing every resting commitment. Applying that principle to perps gives us a useful version of the best of both worlds: a lit book that anyone can inspect, plus private liquidity that can improve the prices available to trade.


## One Order Can Access Both


Consider this sell side:


-


**Private seller:** 20 at $100.05, not publicly displayed.


-


**Displayed seller:** 50 at $100.10, publicly displayed.


An ordinary buyer submits an order for 30 units with a limit of $100.10.


Assuming the orders remain available and the usual checks permit execution, the buyer receives 20 at $100.05 from the private seller, then 10 at $100.10 from the displayed seller. The remaining displayed quantity is 40, and the improvement is five cents on each of the first 20 units.


## Display Still Earns Priority


QFEX needs to give traders a reason to quote publicly.


QFEX’s priority rule starts with price. For an ordinary taking order, a better eligible private price beats a worse displayed price. At the same price, however, displayed orders execute before private orders. Time priority then applies within each price and visibility class.


So the private offer at $100.05 beats the displayed offer at $100.10. If both sellers ask $100.10, the displayed seller executes first, even if the private order arrived earlier. Fees follow the ordinary maker/taker rules.


## Orders for Off-Market Hours


Private orders make sense when confidentiality attracts size or prices that traders would otherwise withhold. On QFEX, our market makers have shown us an increased willingness to quote tighter during weekends and off-market hours using Private Orders than using regular orders, which is why we are willing to give it a shot.


Simply moving existing quotes out of public view would make the displayed book less informative without necessarily improving anyone’s execution.
